questions.stem: Which statement about protons and neutrons is correct?
options: They are each made of two quarks and an electron
They are each made of three smaller particles called quarks
They are fundamental particles with no smaller parts
They are each made of a positron and an electron bound together
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons are not fundamental: each is made of three quarks. Quarks, like electrons, are fundamental particles as far as is known. A neutron is not a proton and an electron stuck together, even though β⁻ decay produces both.

questions.stem: What is the quark make-up of a proton?
options: Two down quarks and one electron
Two up quarks and one down quark
One up quark and two down quarks
Three up quarks
questions.explanation: A proton is uud: two up quarks and one down quark. Its charge is +2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1 e. One up and two down quarks, udd, make a neutron.

questions.stem: Using quark charges of +2/3 e for up and −1/3 e for down, what is the charge of a neutron's quarks added together?
questions.explanation: A neutron is udd, so its charge is +2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0. This is why a neutron is uncharged even though it contains charged quarks. The proton, uud, adds up to +1 e.

questions.stem: What are the charges of the up and down quarks?
options: Up +2/3 e, down −1/3 e
Up +1/3 e, down −2/3 e
Up +1 e, down −1 e
Up +2/3 e, down −2/3 e
questions.explanation: The up quark has charge +2/3 e and the down quark −1/3 e, where e is the size of the electron's charge. These values make the proton (uud) +1 e and the neutron (udd) zero. Quarks are the only known particles with fractional charges.

questions.stem: Which of these particles is not a fundamental particle?
options: Electron
Up quark
Down quark
Neutron
questions.explanation: A neutron is made of three quarks, so it is not fundamental. Electrons and quarks have no known internal structure and are treated as fundamental particles.

questions.stem: A particle made of three up quarks has been observed in high-energy experiments. What is its charge?
questions.explanation: Each up quark has +2/3 e, so three give 3 × 2/3 = +2 e. The +2/3 e answer counts only one quark, and +1 e is the proton's charge, which needs one of the three to be a down quark.

questions.stem: How many up quarks are there in a helium-4 nucleus?
questions.explanation: Helium-4 has 2 protons (uud) and 2 neutrons (udd). The up quarks number 2 × 2 + 2 × 1 = 6. The 12 is the total number of quarks, and 8 counts two up quarks in every nucleon.

questions.stem: How many down quarks are there in a carbon-12 nucleus, which has 6 protons and 6 neutrons?
questions.explanation: Each proton (uud) has one down quark and each neutron (udd) has two: 6 × 1 + 6 × 2 = 18. The total number of quarks is 36, and 12 would mean one down quark in each nucleon.

questions.stem: In β⁻ decay, what change happens to a quark inside the nucleus?
options: An up quark changes into a down quark
An up quark is emitted from the nucleus
A down quark splits into two up quarks
A down quark changes into an up quark
questions.explanation: In β⁻ decay a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud), so one down quark changes into an up quark, and an electron and an antineutrino are emitted. An up quark becoming a down quark is β⁺ decay. Quarks are never emitted singly.

questions.stem: In β⁺ decay, what change happens to a quark inside the nucleus?
options: An up quark joins with an electron
An up quark changes into a down quark
A down quark changes into an up quark
A down quark is emitted as a positron
questions.explanation: In β⁺ decay a proton (uud) becomes a neutron (udd), so one up quark becomes a down quark, and a positron and a neutrino are emitted. The atomic number falls by one while the mass number is unchanged.

questions.stem: In β⁻ decay a down quark (−1/3 e) becomes an up quark (+2/3 e). How is charge conserved?
options: An antineutrino, with charge −1 e, is emitted
A proton, with charge +1 e, is emitted
An electron, with charge −1 e, is emitted
A positron, with charge +1 e, is emitted
questions.explanation: The quark's charge rises from −1/3 e to +2/3 e, an increase of +1 e, so a particle of charge −1 e must be created to keep the total at −1/3 e. That particle is the electron. The antineutrino emitted with it is uncharged.

questions.stem: In β⁺ decay, an up quark changes into a down quark. Which particles are emitted?
options: A positron and a neutrino
An electron and an antineutrino
A positron and an antineutrino
An electron and a neutrino
questions.explanation: The quark's charge falls from +2/3 e to −1/3 e, so a positive particle, the positron, is emitted to conserve charge, along with a neutrino. β⁻ decay emits the electron and antineutrino. The neutrino goes with the positron and the antineutrino with the electron.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 decays by β⁻ emission to nitrogen-14. How do the numbers of up and down quarks in the nucleus change?
options: Both increase by one, because a new nucleon is formed
Neither changes, because the mass number stays at 14
Up quarks increase by one and down quarks decrease by one
Up quarks decrease by one and down quarks increase by one
questions.explanation: A neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud), so one down quark becomes an up quark. The total number of quarks, and so the mass number, is unchanged, but the atomic number rises from 6 to 7. Only the type of one quark changes.

questions.stem: Why is the mass number of a nucleus unchanged by β⁻ or β⁺ decay?
options: A nucleon is lost and another is gained from the surroundings
Only the type of one quark changes, so the number of nucleons stays the same
The emitted electron or positron has exactly the mass of one nucleon
The neutrino carries away the mass of the nucleon that is lost
questions.explanation: In beta decay one quark changes type, turning a neutron into a proton or the reverse. The number of nucleons, and so the mass number A, stays the same, while Z changes by one. Electrons and positrons have about 1/1840 of a nucleon's mass.

questions.stem: A free proton never undergoes β⁺ decay, yet protons inside some nuclei do. Why?
options: A free proton is held together too tightly by the strong nuclear force
A neutron has more mass than a proton, so the energy must come from the nucleus
A free proton has no down quarks, so it cannot change into a neutron
A free proton cannot emit a neutrino unless other nucleons are close by
questions.explanation: A neutron is slightly more massive than a proton, so changing a free proton into a neutron, positron and neutrino would need energy. Inside a proton-rich nucleus, the change can lower the nucleus's total energy, which supplies it. A proton already contains a down quark, and it changes an up quark in β⁺ decay.

questions.stem: Which describes a neutrino?
options: A neutral particle with the same mass as a neutron, found in every nucleus
A charged particle with a very small mass that is stopped by thin paper
An uncharged particle of light emitted when an electron changes energy level
An uncharged particle with a very small mass that interacts very weakly with matter
questions.explanation: Neutrinos have no charge, a tiny mass and interact so weakly that most pass straight through Earth. They are not nucleons and are not found inside nuclei. A packet of light emitted by an atom is a photon, not a neutrino.

questions.stem: Early measurements showed that electrons from β⁻ decay of one nuclide had a continuous range of energies up to a maximum. Why did this suggest another particle was emitted?
options: If only the electron were emitted, the charge of the nucleus would not change in the decay
If only the electron were emitted, the nucleus would have to lose one nucleon in each decay
If only the electron were emitted, energy conservation would give every electron the same energy
If only the electron were emitted, it would always have more energy than the decay released
questions.explanation: Each decay of a given nuclide releases the same energy, so if the electron and the recoiling nucleus were the only products, the electrons would all have the same energy. A spread of energies meant an unseen particle was sharing the energy, as Pauli proposed in 1930. That particle is the antineutrino.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 β⁻ decay releases 0.156 MeV of kinetic energy. An electron from one decay is detected with 0.050 MeV. Ignoring the nucleus's small recoil energy, how much energy did the antineutrino carry?
questions.explanation: The energy released is shared between the electron and the antineutrino, so the antineutrino has 0.156 − 0.050 = 0.106 MeV. Adding the two gives 0.206 MeV, which would break energy conservation. The electron gets the full 0.156 MeV only in the rare decays where the antineutrino carries almost nothing.

questions.stem: In a β⁻ decay the electron and the recoiling nucleus are observed not to move in exactly opposite directions. What does this show?
options: The nucleus must have been moving quickly before the decay occurred
A third particle carries momentum, since the total must be conserved
Momentum is not conserved in nuclear decays, unlike in collisions
The electron's path is bent by the charge of the nucleus it leaves
questions.explanation: If a nucleus at rest split into only two particles, conservation of momentum would send them off in exactly opposite directions. Since they do not, a third, undetected particle, the antineutrino, must carry the missing momentum. Momentum is conserved in all nuclear reactions.

questions.stem: Why are neutrinos so difficult to detect?
options: They are charged, so magnetic fields steer them away from detectors
They are only produced in nuclear reactors, which shield them heavily
They interact so weakly with matter that almost all pass through a detector
They travel so slowly that they decay before reaching any detector
questions.explanation: Neutrinos have no charge and interact only very weakly, so most pass through the whole Earth without any interaction. Detectors must be very large to catch the occasional one. They are produced in huge numbers by the Sun as well as by reactors.

questions.stem: In which pair of decays are a neutrino and an antineutrino respectively emitted?
options: β⁺ decay emits both; β⁻ decay emits neither of them
β⁺ decay emits a neutrino; β⁻ decay emits an antineutrino
β⁻ decay emits a neutrino; β⁺ decay emits an antineutrino
α decay emits a neutrino; γ decay emits an antineutrino
questions.explanation: A β⁺ decay emits a positron and a neutrino, and a β⁻ decay emits an electron and an antineutrino. In each case the antimatter particle is paired with a matter particle. Alpha and gamma decay do not emit neutrinos.

questions.stem: In 1919 Rutherford bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → X + ¹₁H. What is the nuclide X?
options: ¹⁷₈O
¹⁸₉F
¹⁷₉F
¹⁶₈O
questions.explanation: Mass numbers: 14 + 4 = A + 1, so A = 17. Atomic numbers: 7 + 2 = Z + 1, so Z = 8, which is oxygen. This was the first artificial transmutation, changing one element into another. ¹⁸₉F would mean no proton was emitted.

questions.stem: Chadwick's 1932 experiment used the reaction ⁹₄Be + ⁴₂He → ¹²₆C + X. What is X?
options: A neutron
A proton
An electron
A positron
questions.explanation: Balancing mass numbers, 9 + 4 = 12 + 1, and atomic numbers, 4 + 2 = 6 + 0, so X has A = 1 and Z = 0: a neutron. Its discovery confirmed that nuclei contain uncharged particles as well as protons. A proton would need Z = 1.

questions.stem: Cobalt-60, used in radiotherapy, is made by placing cobalt-59 in a nuclear reactor. Which process produces it?
options: Cobalt-59 captures a neutron, a type of artificial transmutation
Cobalt-59 undergoes β⁻ decay, a type of spontaneous transmutation
Cobalt-59 captures a proton, raising its atomic number by one
Cobalt-59 undergoes fission, splitting off a lighter nuclide
questions.explanation: A reactor supplies a large flux of neutrons. Cobalt-59 absorbs one, ⁵⁹₂₇Co + ¹₀n → ⁶⁰₂₇Co, becoming cobalt-60. This is a managed, artificial transmutation. Capturing a proton would change the element to nickel.

questions.stem: Why are neutrons especially effective at causing artificial transmutation?
options: They travel faster than light, so they pass the electron cloud
They are uncharged, so the nucleus does not repel them
They are much heavier than alpha particles, so they hit harder
They are positively charged, so the electrons attract them inward
questions.explanation: A neutron has no charge, so it can approach a nucleus without electrostatic repulsion, even at low speed. Alpha particles and protons are repelled by the positive nucleus and need high energies. A neutron is about a quarter of the mass of an alpha particle.

questions.stem: What was the early universe composed of, before stars formed?
options: Mostly iron, with lighter elements formed later by fission
Equal amounts of all the elements now found on Earth
Mostly carbon and oxygen, with hydrogen formed later in stars
Mostly hydrogen, with helium and traces of other light elements
questions.explanation: The early universe was mostly hydrogen, with about a quarter helium by mass and traces of other light elements. All heavier elements, including the carbon, oxygen and iron in our bodies, were made later by nuclear processes in stars and when stars were destroyed.

questions.stem: What is the main source of the Sun's energy?
options: Fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium in its core
Fission of uranium nuclei in its core
Burning of hydrogen gas with oxygen at its surface
Radioactive decay of iron throughout its interior
questions.explanation: In the Sun's hot, dense core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, converting a little mass into energy. Chemical burning could only power the Sun for thousands of years, and the Sun contains very little uranium.

questions.stem: Carbon in stars is made when helium-4 nuclei fuse. How many helium-4 nuclei fuse to make one carbon-12 nucleus?
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and each helium-4 nucleus has 2 of each, so 12/4 = 3 helium-4 nuclei are needed. Fusing two gives beryllium-8, which is unstable. This helium fusion happens in older stars whose cores have run out of hydrogen.

questions.stem: Why can fusion in a star's core release energy only for elements up to about iron?
options: A star's core is never hot enough to fuse any nucleus heavier than helium
Iron nuclei repel each other magnetically, which stops any further fusion
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron, so fusing heavier nuclei absorbs energy
Nuclei heavier than iron are radioactive, so they decay before they can fuse
questions.explanation: Fusion releases energy when the product is more tightly bound per nucleon than the reactants. Binding energy per nucleon rises up to a peak near iron, then falls, so fusing nuclei beyond iron takes in energy instead. A massive star's core builds up iron and can no longer release energy by fusion.

questions.stem: Where were most of the elements heavier than iron, such as gold and uranium, formed?
options: In the cores of Sun-like stars, by fusing hydrogen into heavier nuclei
In the first few minutes after the Big Bang, by fusing helium
In the Earth's core, by fission of even heavier nuclei
In the late stages and destruction of stars, by capturing neutrons
questions.explanation: Making nuclei beyond iron absorbs energy, so they are not made by ordinary fusion. They form when nuclei capture neutrons, in the late stages of stars and especially in the destruction of stars, such as supernova explosions and neutron star collisions. The early universe cooled too quickly to make elements this heavy.

questions.stem: Where did the carbon and oxygen atoms in your body originally come from?
options: The first few minutes of the Big Bang, along with hydrogen
Radioactive decay of uranium in the rocks of the early Earth
Chemical reactions in Earth's early atmosphere and oceans
Fusion inside stars, which scattered them into space as they died
questions.explanation: Carbon and oxygen are made by helium fusion inside stars. When those stars shed their outer layers or exploded, the elements were spread through space and later became part of new stars, planets and living things. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms but cannot create new elements.

questions.stem: The Sun emits enormous numbers of neutrinos. Which part of its fusion process produces them?
options: Electrons dropping between energy levels in hot gas
Helium nuclei splitting apart in the Sun's outer layers
Protons changing into neutrons as hydrogen becomes helium
Neutrons changing into protons as helium becomes hydrogen
questions.explanation: A helium-4 nucleus has 2 protons and 2 neutrons, but it is made from hydrogen nuclei, which are protons. Two protons must change into neutrons, each emitting a positron and a neutrino, as in β⁺ decay. Electron transitions emit photons, not neutrinos.

questions.stem: Fusing deuterium and tritium releases 17.6 MeV from 5 nucleons, while fission of uranium-235 by a neutron releases about 200 MeV from 236 nucleons. About how many times more energy per nucleon does the fusion release?
options: About 0.25 times
About 47 times
About 4 times
About 11 times
questions.explanation: Fusion gives 17.6/5 ≈ 3.5 MeV per nucleon, and fission gives 200/236 ≈ 0.85 MeV per nucleon, so fusion releases about 4 times as much per nucleon. This is because a greater percentage of the mass is converted into energy. Comparing 200 with 17.6 directly gives about 11, which ignores the numbers of nucleons.
